AI Twitter Recap Meta Releases Muse Spark Open, the Top-Scoring US Open-Weight Model Release : Meta released Muse Spark Open, an 816B-total / 42B-active MoE with a 1M-token context window. It accepts text, image, video and audio input and is aimed at coding, long-horizon agents and multi-step reasoning ( announcement , Wang thread ). Lineage : Jack Rae says it was the first base model trained under the new MSL org, with additional training for the open release ( Rae ). Several posters describe it as roughly Muse Spark 1.2 level ( Yuchen Jin , TimDarcet ). License : The weights ship under the custom Muse Model License. It requires “Built with Muse Spark Open” attribution and a separate agreement for Model-as-a-Service businesses with more than $20M in annual revenue ( AA ). Nathan Lambert called the license “trash” ( natolambert ). Architecture : According to vLLM, the model has 62 decoder layers, all MoE, with 256 experts per layer and 8 active per token. A latent-MoE pooler projects the hidden state from 8,192 to 4,096 for expert computation and back again. Attention is hybrid: 46 layers use a 2,048-token sliding window and 16 attend to the full context. Image and video go through a Perception Encoder, and audio uses a separate 118M encoder ( vLLM arch ). Design comparison : Elie Bakouch notes that Muse is the only major US open model without shared experts. It also uses gated residuals, about 9 norms per layer and muP-like multipliers, including a router factor of 1/sqrt(number of experts) ( overview ). Independent measurement : Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index. That ranks it first among US open-weight models but behind GLM-5.3 (45) and Kimi K3 (44) ( AA , Rundown ). Strengths : It uses 40k output tokens per index task, the fewest among the nine highest-scoring open models. It also leads open models on AA-Omniscience (25). Weaknesses : It ranks last among those nine on the index’s four agentic evaluations. GLM-5.3’s entire 6-point lead comes from that agentic segment. Pricing and deployment : Launch pricing on Together, Fireworks and Baseten is $1.25/$4.25 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.15 cached input). AA calculates this at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Together offers a free endpoint until Oct 18 ( Together ). Hardware footprint : BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. The NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts and comes to about 530GB, which runs on 4× Blackwell Ultra, 8× H200, or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios via MLX ( AA , Meta ). Ecosystem : llama.cpp had GGUF support on day 0 ( Delangue ), and Unsloth published quants, with UD-IQ1_S at 176GB ( Unsloth ). vLLM day-0 stack : vLLM support covers NVIDIA, AMD MI355X (FP8 and MXFP4) and TPU ( vLLM ). TPU throughput : Megakernels with DSpark speculation (acceptance length 6) exceed 650 tok/s on 4 TPU v7 chips and 960 tok/s on 8 ( hardware ). Speculator : Inferact trained a block-diffusion DSpark drafter that proposes up to 7 tokens per pass ( speculator ). LoRA RL : LoRA GRPO uses verl for training and vLLM for rollouts. Over 150 steps on 16 GB300s, AIME-2024 mean@8 rose from 0.56 to 0.85, with train-rollout KL around 2×10⁻⁴ ( RL ). Reception : Lambert says the release cuts the US–China open-model gap by about half ( natolambert ). Teortaxes calls it “grim at this param count” with “obsolete attention” and notes that Spark 1.3 is substantially stronger; these are attributed opinions ( teortaxes , Spark 1.3 comparison ). Other Model Launches: Nemotron 3.5, MAI-Base-2, Gemini 4 Argon, Image Models NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL : The model is a 120B / 12B-active hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE VLM with a 1M-token context window and native MTP ( NVIDIA ). Training recipe : The tech summary describes a 1T-token distillation from a larger Nemotron 3 teacher, followed by agentic SWE mid-training on 65.4B tokens at 256K context. Post-training uses multi-teacher MOPD, and a final MTP-boosting step raises acceptance length by 21.8% to 4.61 ( Gordić ). Claimed results : NVIDIA reports 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro and 4,856 output tok/s per GPU on GB200. Independent evals : AA scores Super VL 26, the leading US open model before Muse, with NVFP4 within 0.1 points of BF16. The companion Nemotron 3.5 Bolt (74B-A9B, native 2-bit, 24GB) scores 21 ( AA ). Pricing : CoreWeave charges $0.25/$1.50 per 1M input/output tokens ( CoreWeave ). Microsoft MAI-Base-2 : Microsoft says it has a roughly 3T-parameter pre-trained base model, with post-training results to follow. It claims to match DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base on held-out code with 12× less training compute ( Suleyman , compute claim ). items.title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
items.content: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from " people with knowledge of the matter ". Key things I learned from the article: Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn" Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power" Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11% This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine): The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones. When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending. Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter. Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter! Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" ( previously ) in these communications to their investors. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic

Crossing the Threshold: How OpenAI and Anthropic Approach Autonomy and Safety in Financial Agents
items.content: OpenAI’s Joseph Kim talks about the threshold phenomenon at AIE NY today. One of the key themes at the AI Engineer New York conference this week was how to balance agent autonomy with security and safety . Both frontier labs and financial firms focused on this issue in their presentations this week. The main lesson: safe autonomy depends on where you put controls and human judgment , rather than how many restrictions you impose. Sponsor: Build shopping into your agent with shop.dev Adding commerce to an agent usually means rebuilding search and checkout from scratch. shop.dev gives you a single API for shopping in any agent or app. One connection gives you access to over a billion products with current price and availability, instant sign in with Shop, and one-tap Shop Pay checkout that happens right in the conversation. It’s open to any developer, with no account or key needed to try it. → Try shop.dev today Joseph Kim , Head of ChatGPT for Financial Services at OpenAI, gave a keynote at AIE New York today. (We also did a special podcast with Kim, which will be released shortly.) He talked about reliability and a “threshold of usefulness,” which he said is “the point where a model becomes capable and reliable enough to save you time.” Kim argued that ever-growing model capability will soon take financial analysts over the threshold and allow them to delegate more work to agents. He made some specific predictions about AI’s role in finance in 2027. Not only will the financial industry rely less on Excel and PowerPoint next year, he claimed, but agents will be good enough to do “investment idea generation and trading.” The “rising tide” of model capabilities is also leading to better traceability . “In finance, you need to be able to check where a number came from and understand the context around it,” said Kim. “We wanted that review to be a natural part of the [ChatGPT for Financial Services] experience. These are the kind of product details that help turn a model’s capabilities into work that someone can use. ” Joseph Kim at AIE NY; photo by Richard MacManus As for when a human needs to be in the loop, Kim framed this as a product design decision. “How would the interface change? What would the user still need to control, review, or approve? Those are product design questions you can start working on now.” Balancing AI Safety and Innovation at a Hedge Fund John Feminella , SVP Architecture at the hedge fund Two Sigma , is tackling the exact kinds of product design questions Kim referenced. In a keynote, he talked about five of the controls they’ve implemented to keep agents in check without limiting model capabilities. Feminella argued that safety and innovation shouldn’t be viewed as opposite ends of a spectrum. He was especially critical of “approval fatigue,” where a person approving everything can hold back innovation — and also introduce risk, if they’re not fully paying attention to all the decisions they’re required to make. At Two Sigma, they’ve implemented a set of controls , which he defined as “guardrails and shared capabilities that let teams move in ways that don’t hinder what they’re trying to do.” The controls are composable, meaning “each one does one job and then together they let us run agents with real autonomy at an appropriate level of safety.” One of the controls is to use auto-mode classifiers , which Feminella said “make decisions about routine calls and then send a person only the requests that are most important, the ones that are most likely to make a difference.” Classifiers can be used for ambiguous cases, whereas deterministic rules are better for clear cases. Anthropic: Give agents context, then define the boundaries of trust Anthropic’s presentation outlined a similar framework, in its case with the goal of building “trust” into financial agentic workflows. Last month, Anthropic announced Claude for Financial Advisors , allowing financial advisors to connect their systems to Claude and a set of workflow skills. At AIE this week, Belinda Neal , Managing Director of Financial Services at Anthropic, explained why Anthropic has partnered with financial firms on the new product. “Every so often, a model crosses a threshold. And when it does, a wave of working changes.” Neal’s colleague Keon Shahab , who works on applied AI at Anthropic, then talked about “building the trust layer for the agents.” He said this involves three steps: “Who the agent is acting as with an identity and permissions layer . How we can sandbox and determine the approval layer of the agent, so that someone is signing off before it acts. And lastly, how we know the agent will still work once we adjust any variables over time.” Shahab illustrated the boundary between proposing and acting with a trade break investigation agent, which would recommend an order amendment for human approval. “We want it [the agent] to just propose new amendments to our orders data, not actually make those amendments,” he said. “By building once with a foundational layer that you trust , you can work at speed to deploy many agents at scale,” Shahab concluded. Bloomberg: Enforce security outside the model As Head of Architecture & Emerging Technologies in the Office of the CTO at Bloomberg, Andrey Rybka has the responsibility to balance autonomy and scale at the company. In a presentation today at AIE, Rybka talked about a series of real-life events where agents caused havoc — and the defenses that can help prevent it . These include scoped identities and credentials, controls over tool calls, outbound traffic restrictions, audit trails, budgets, and kill switches. items.title: Lab-in-the-Loop at Compute Speed — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
items.content: A few years ago I stumbled upon Leash Bio’s Substack , and was hooked. Be it their Kaggle competition that showed that no, we really haven’t solved protein-ligand binding , or their crazy discovery that knowing a molecule’s author is perhaps all you need to know to predict how good it is . Their substack — or at least Owl Posting ’s 1 deep dive on them — should be required reading for any scientist trying to do chemistry with AI. So I was super excited to finally be able to sit down with Ian Quigley from Leash Bio, and pick his brain. Leash specializes in DNA Encoded Libraries (aka “DELs”), a way of collecting ridiculously high-throughput interaction data between proteins and small molecules. 2 Before I discovered Leash, I had heard nothing but horror stories from DEL users. And yet, Ian and friends somehow found a way to tame the beast, extracting clean and reproducible data that is just perfect for large scale modeling. Without teasing too much, the answer comes down to epistemic rigor, and an incredible conviction that you just have to Do The Thing. It gets even better! Near the end of this episode, Ian teases something his team was just playing with when we recorded: an AI playground for agents to do verifiable scientific reasoning. They discovered the data they had spent the last few years collecting could provide tens of thousands of “lab-in-the-loop” simulations, just what an agent needs for scientific RL. Two months later, it’s matured into Minos, and today they’re releasing a full preprint , blog , and open dataset . We’ll be releasing a lightning podcast in a few days with an update. Stay tuned! We had a blast with Ian, probably one of our most fun episodes to date. For both complete chemistry novices and expert AI x Bio practitioners, we think you’ll get something out of this. Enjoy! We covered: Why DELs traumatize everyone who touches them, and how Leash puts dozens of barcodes on each molecule to catch proteins that bind the DNA instead of the drug. Ian’s rule that biology only scales two ways: taking pictures and sequencing DNA. The Kaggle competition : about 4B measurements from a basement and about 2,000 teams, with nobody beating chance on an unseen chemical library. Also why Leash quietly feared co-folding would make them obsolete. Clever Hans in ChEMBL : models can guess a molecule’s chemist from its structure, and “who made it” predicts activity about as well as the structure does. Hermes , trained only on Leash’s own data, keeping pace with Boltz on public benchmarks. Plus the BRD4 molecule Boltz had already seen in the PDB. Breaking the pocket : engineering protein mutants at scale after catching Hermes memorizing “nicknames” for proteins instead of binding sites. Lumacaftor -like hits as an accidental detector for misfolded proteins. The agent sandbox : LLMs that reason about SAR in plain English, hunting for the best binders among 6.5M molecules on a budget of 100. The Recursion mafia, and why its alumni companies all rhyme. The Kosuri paradox : if you can collect the data, why do you need the model? Going from a DEL hit to good mouse PKPD in six months on an inflammation program, and the case for pills over antibodies on cytokine targets. What stops a better-funded lab from outscaling them, and Ian’s by-fiat wish for massively parallel purification. 1 The hands-down best bio blogger on the internet. 2 As always, the secret here is to map your problem to a combinatorial library and a readout using Next Generation Sequencing. We talk about this in depth in the podcast!

AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
items.content: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks. Via Hacker News Tags: computer-history , game-design , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , coding-agents

items.content: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. Via Hacker News Tags: git , migrations , version-control , ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , agentic-engineering

Last month, Dyna made waves by announcing Dyna-2 , a world-action model pre-trained on one million hours of human video, claiming several new scaling laws on human data across four orders of magnitude . From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung , Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. How Anthropic’s Dynamic Workflows Coordinate Claude Agents
items.content: CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, at AI Engineer NYC today. The AI Engineer New York 2026 conference kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents . Of particular interest was a brand new feature, announced on Friday , called dynamic workflows — or simply “flows,” as the presenters repeatedly called it. Flows are defined as “a new type of multiagent orchestration, built for your most ambitious workloads.” CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall , both Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic , began by invoking some operating system projects of the past — from Ken Thompson building the original Unix operating system, through to Linux evolving from one person (Linus Torvalds) to layers of trusted maintainers . The lesson: agents need the same level of organization in order to do the types of big, ambitious projects Anthropic envisions for dynamic workflows. Sponsored by Union.ai Build a sovereign AI factory The best engineering teams are building AI factories where they own and control not only their data, compute, and infrastructure, but also a durable runtime on their cloud. Union.ai gives your workflows the durability to adapt and right-size infra resources and recover from failures without re-running completed work. Get started directly through AWS Marketplace and try Union.ai free for 30 days . To learn more, visit us at AI Engineer New York booth #48. “I think a lot of us who are orchestrating and managing lots of agents now might start to feel this feeling of being the bottleneck and being the breaking point as we have lots of agents contributing tons and tons of PRs,” Avilla said. “And we’re sitting there in our GitHub trying to approve PRs and make sure that everything works as expected.” From agent rosters to dynamic workflows The pair noted that dynamic workflows began in Claude Code as the “a harness for every task” concept. But flows can run longer than a single agent or a roster. The basic idea is that Claude chooses the organization of agents. “Flows are essentially the next version of multi-agent orchestration,” said Stall, “where you can let Claude fully orchestrate the entirety of its own multi-agent topology.” The way this works is that the lead agent creates a plan for how it wants to accomplish tasks. Claude then writes an orchestration program, which launches agents, collects results, and manages information flow. Image via Anthropic Previously, Claude Managed Agents required developers to configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents. With dynamic workflows, Claude itself determines how to divide and orchestrate the work. “Across multiple different phases of the multi-agent orchestration, it’s able to accomplish discrete, verifiable units of work without you having to manage any of the interconnections between these things,” Stall said. That said, Avilla noted that the user can introduce specialist sub-agents if they wish. “It’s also possible in the agent config to pass in pre-configured sub-agents,” he said. All of this is available in Claude Console , the interface used by developers accessing Claude through API — the whole point of Claude Managed Agents. Claude Console, where Managed Agents is located. The presenters then showed a relatively simple workflow of a stock watchlist scanner. Although this was far removed from the big, ambitious projects Anthropic is encouraging, it did illustrate the basic pattern : a scan phase distributed individual tickers to agents with isolated contexts , and a later review phase examined the findings before producing a report. Q&A: Budgets and the limits of self-improvement The audience Q&A surfaced a number of potential problems. One audience member asked how Claude decides how many agents a task needs , and could a simple ticker scan trigger hundreds of sub-agents? “The answer really is evals and lower defaults ,” Stall replied, noting that ambitious tasks generally require explicitly encouraging greater parallelization. One enduring concern with agent orchestration is maintaining control over your token budget . Someone asked whether the lead agent knows how much money it has available? Stall replied that the model does not know its budget while running, but that developers can set a session budget. He added that informing models of their budgets could make the agents “a little bit anxious,” which elicited chuckles from the audience. Scanner in the stock watchlist example. A related question was how can developers make repeated flows cheaper and more efficient over time? Outside of asking Claude to examine the costs incurred, Avilla suggested another relatively new feature be used: dreaming . In the documentation , “dreaming” is defined as a research preview feature. A dream “reads an existing memory store alongside past session transcripts, then produces a new, reorganized memory store, ” with duplicates merged, “stale or contradicted entries” replaced, and “new insights surfaced.” Avilla described dreaming in the flow context as being able to “crystallize and basically improve the memory store that is related to those sessions.” For the stock watchlist example, someone asked whether the watchlist flow can improve itself? For example, recognize that its scanning model is inadequate and change the next scheduled run? Stall said this wasn’t built in, but he and Avilla suggested hill-climbing and dreaming could be used to improve the loop. The brain/hands conceptual overview of Managed Agents. What about visibility into the actions of the sub-agents , another audience member asked. Avilla replied that yes, developers can always inspect that through graphing functionality inside Claude Cons

items.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
items.content: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448 , which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. A sampling profiler Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing , and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling . Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first. I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library. If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS): sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234 Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this: It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this , and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI. 3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14 Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase. Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories. Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release: uv self update Then I installed the stable 3.15 release: uv python install 3.15 And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version: uv python pin --global 3.15 Now the following reports 3.15 as the version: uv run python --version I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install . I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this: uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15 Then I can confirm the version like this: datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq Highlights from Python 3.11 The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported . My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11. Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available! Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio . 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout() , and several more new features. datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc . Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including: setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python. create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step() , value() , inverse() , and finalize() methods. blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row. You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this! Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system . I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround. I've also updated my click-app , datasette-plugin , python-lib , and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15. items.content: I remember hearing a while ago that Dwarf Fortress didn't use version control. That fact has been lodged in my head, because given its inherent complexity I have trouble imagining a codebase that would benefit from version control more . That's art. I went looking and I'm sad to report that the days without version control appear to have ended. Quoting Tarn Adams over time: March 2013: "I don't use version control -- I didn't like the feeling of having the code get committed into a black box thingy with no immediate upside" March 2016: "I don’t even use version control. If you don’t know what that is then you’re not gonna yell at me. If you even know what version control is you’re gonna be like, ‘You don’t use version control? You don’t use source control? What is wrong with you? How can you even work? I’m just not cut out for it, in a sense. It’s been 15 years, so the reasons have change over time, but that’s my current understanding of it." March 2023: "I've got Discord channels to check and version control stuff to use now, so the process is definitely a little more involved" That March 2023 quote comes from an interview about the release on Steam which made them millionaires . items.content: When you think of robotics and AI, you probably first think of full humanoid robots like Figure’s AI-powered machines and 1X’s NEO home robots . Those may well be the future, but arguably more important in 2026 is industrial robots — which are typically not humanoids. Standard Bots claims to be “America’s largest AI-native industrial robot manufacturer.” It recently raised $200 million at a $1 billion valuation, in a series C round led by General Catalyst and RoboStrategy, a fund focused on robotics. Its customers include NASA, Amazon and Lockheed Martin. We spoke to Evan Beard , co-founder and CEO, and Leif Jentoft , Head of AI, to find out more about Standard Bots’ AI stack and how its models work. To set the scene, Standard Bots’ industrial robot arms are designed for tasks such as machine tending, welding, and assembly. Here’s a quick demo by Jentoft: Pretrained models and task-specific adaptation According to Beard, Standard Bots has a shared base model that customers adapt through demonstrations and fine-tuning. Jentoft added that Standard Bots runs a range of models , including a zero-shot perception system for machine tending. Beard says its largest model is in the low billions of parameters — so it’s not that large by frontier lab standards. “We believe data quality matters far more than raw volume,” said Jentoft, “and we focus on getting the most out of targeted data rather than chasing the largest possible dataset.” (This matches the “bitterest lesson” of Jev creator Diogo Almeida , who told us recently that the right task and the right data can matter more than compute.) “Our market access gives us unique access to the highest value data,” he added. “ In-situ interventions can fix an edge case with a few dozen examples.” Setting up part identification with ClickFind. Beard notes that Standard Bots focuses on short-horizon tasks to meet production requirements for cycle time and reliability. The company uses conventional programming for parts of a workflow that don’t require learned behavior. Model training happens in the cloud but inference runs locally , said Beard. What does the model do exactly? I asked Jentoft what the learned model does in a typical robot routine, and which parts of the workflow use conventional programming? As an example, he brought up its machine-tending solution for high-mix manufacturing. “We’ve built a zero-shot system that lets a user tell the robot which parts to look for on a given task. The model handles perception — locating and identifying the parts — while conventional programming handles the motion and the cell logic around it.” Here’s a demonstration of the machine-tending: “Our backbone for this task is trained on over a billion images , which is what lets the robot distinguish between lighting conditions, material types, and an object versus its background,” Jentoft said. The Full AI Stack Back in April, we had Applied Intuition on the podcast to talk about “Physical AI” and how it differs from on-screen AI. One of the learnings was that the Physical AI isn’t just constrained by model intelligence: the hard part is deploying models onto real hardware , under safety, latency, power, cost, and reliability constraints. But for Standard Bots, that can also be a strength, since it controls the “full stack” from software to hardware. Jentoft points out that it controls the robotic arm, end effector, control system, and AI. “That lets us co-optimize the models and the control policies ,” he said. “Despite claims elsewhere, no model today is truly hardware-agnostic, and co-optimizing low-level control and higher-level functions is a major advantage for both performance and iteration speed.” Skild , a company aiming to build “general purpose robotic intelligence,” might quibble with the hardware-agnostic claim — its goal is to achieve cross-hardware generalization . On-prem inference: sensors, edge GPUs, and ‘action chunks’ Beard had mentioned that inference is done locally, which is especially important for its core customers: factories. “For factories, which is most of what we’re doing right now — and certainly so much opportunity that we see there — this is something where you need to do inference on-premise ,” he said. An AI agent building a machine-tending routine. For machine tending, the model identifies parts while conventional programming handles motion. Jentoft also described how models can generate actions that feed into the robot’s control system. “Wrist cameras and other sensors feed raw pixels and signals into the system over internal gigabit Ethernet , routed internally so no cables tangle,” he explained. “ GPUs at the edge process that data to generate action chunks , which stream to low-level control.” He reiterated that inference is run on-premises deliberately. “Cloud compute for robotics is operationally extremely hard — most factories and warehouses don’t have reliable internet , and that’s even more true for mobile robots. Uptime is crucial to customer acceptance, so we keep the loop local.” Production failures and fleet learning Standard Bots uses simulation where it can, but Beard says some production tasks — including those involving liquids, suction, or cutting flexible material — are difficult to reproduce in current simulators. Real-world demonstrations are another part of the learning process. AI Twitter Recap Decision Models Become a Product Category The pattern : Several vendors shipped “decision” models on the same day. These return typed answers (probabilities, picks from a list, scores) in a single forward pass instead of free text. Jev is the reference point everyone benchmarks against, and @scaling01 remarked on how fast the format spread. OpenAI Decisions API : Three request types: probability that a condition is true, pick from a list, or score against levels. It accepts text and images, runs on GPT-6 Luna, costs $0.10/M input tokens with no output charge, and is “up to 10x faster” by OpenAI’s own figure ( @LearnOpenCV ). items.title: Why AlphaFold Didn't Solve Protein Folding — Pushmeet Kohli, Google DeepMind & Sal Candido, Biohub
items.content: From the Bitter Lesson of AI scaling to the unsolved mysteries of protein folding , Google DeepMind’s Pushmeet Kohli and Biohub’s Sal Candido are rethinking what it takes to build AI that truly understands biology. In this special panel moderated by Brandon Anderson , they explore why AlphaFold’s breakthrough was only the beginning , why scaling compute and data alone won’t solve biology, and how the next generation of AI models could transform our understanding of proteins, cells, and human disease. We go deep on the future of AI-driven biology : finding scaling laws in biological data, the tradeoffs between scientific intuition and general-purpose architectures, why protein structure prediction is far from solved, and what it would take to build predictive models of living systems. Pushmeet reflects on the lessons behind AlphaFold , the limits of human interpretability, and whether future frontier models could understand other AI systems better than we can. Sal explains why protein language models may already contain scientific knowledge we haven’t unlocked, how biological modeling must move beyond individual proteins, and why achieving Biohub’s mission to cure all disease requires thinking in terms of 10x breakthroughs rather than incremental improvements. We discuss: The Bitter Lesson for biology : why scaling compute and data isn’t enough Why finding the right scaling law matters more than blindly increasing model size How low-quality metagenomic data can improve protein language models Why AI researchers optimize for available data instead of the most important scientific problems Lessons from DeepMind on balancing modeling, data generation, and items.content: Deno is joining Cloudflare The Deno team released the first version of celld back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers. Today, Cloudflare are acquiring Deno outright, with the goal of building on celld to "make workerd self-hosting a first-class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model" (see the Cloudflare blog .) The bad news is that Deno itself will not be maintained by Cloudflare beyond the next year: We will support the Deno runtime for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates. After that year we will end our development of the Deno runtime. Deno will remain open source, and we welcome others who want to continue its development. Deno (and Node.js) creator Ryan Dahl explained that decision in a comment on Hacker News: It's a joint decision and I agree with it. I'm most invested in its success and have put the most work into it - and I no longer think it's where I can do the most important work. There are some good ideas in Deno and it's well engineered - but it ultimately is not solving big problems. It has been sucked into the gravity well of node compatibility, which forces it to behave exactly as Node does. Why reimplement Node? It works. Marginal performance or UX or security benefits are not enough. I'm interested in building powerful new abstractions. celld has been working remarkably well, depending only on object storage for coordination and persistence. It is not just a slightly different API to interact with the file system or network - it's an entirely new model for server development. My favorite feature of Deno has long been the permissions system, where you can run a Deno script and specify exactly which files and folders it can read and write to, and which network hosts it can access. Node.js has a similar permissions model these days, added in Node v20.0.0 in April 2023 and declared stable in Node v22.13.0 in January 2025. They don't yet support allow-listing specific network hosts though - networking is either on or off. Via Hacker News Tags: cloudfront , javascript , nodejs , ryan-dahl , sandboxing , deno

items.title: I expect rapid progress but not towards general superintelligence
items.content: I’ve often been surprised when I hear from top researchers in industry that they think AI will be better than them at their job in a few years, and I didn’t really know why I doubted it. The explanation I arrived at is that researchers are seeing this massive acceleration in the infra and engineering capabilities of the models. I fully agree that the models will be superhuman distributed GPU engineers in a few years. This will make experimentation and tinkering with the formulation of the models far easier, but it will not make our models dramatically different in nature. In some ways, Ilya was early in his declaration of AI being in the era of research . Research is much easier today now that we have coding agents. This ease is through a different form of work that is flexible and engaging, which signals the start of an era where good ideas can be much more valuable than good execution in software. Subscribe now We’re very early on this path. It’s also not the first transition the field has seen across the balance in if AI is more “research” or “engineering.” Before deep learning took off, AI was also far more of a research endeavor. Today, the best researchers are well-known to be judged by their ability to implement and scale their ideas in complex infrastructure. We’re about to go through a massive acceleration over a few years where the bottleneck is less and less engineering again. Some call this RSI, but a more grounded form is simply “parallelized, AI-assisted language modeling.” You don’t need to buy into takeoff scenarios to see just how much infrastructure improvements are coming, and how this’ll change the nature of working in AI. The goal of this piece is to give an overview on why this engineering acceleration will happen, and touch on what it won’t quite fix. This’ll be a massive boon for diffusion of the technology into the economy, even if we don’t get economically valuable superhuman traits outside of math and coding. A lot of this near-term progress comes from scaling the inference-time compute we have with current tools, rather than dramatic step-changes in how good the models are at research. Share Many pieces of the AI training and inference stack are very verifiable. Training metrics like tokens per second per GPU, which is just training speed. Inference metrics look like tokens per prompt, FLOPs per token, or really just cost per answer. Both of these are very optimizable, especially as there are established sub-problems and architecture trade-offs which can improve them. I expect AI agents to help optimize this process end-to-end in a few years, where our inference capabilities get very close to the underlying maximum compute possible on our accelerators like GPUs. Over the previous few years, the gains companies can make on inference efficiency were already giant, e.g. saving like 10-30% on cost to serve a model after announcing it at a certain price point. This entire stack will compound, and I expect the effective cost of model intelligence to decline near-exponentially over the coming years (potentially faster than recent trends). This low-hanging fruit of efficiency should take only a few years to capture. The longer term will be co-design of accelerators and models on longer timelines, which give extra orders of magnitude in efficiency on top of the flexible GPU platform. During this time of rapid efficiency gains, the flexibility of the GPU should be king, as the exploration space in architecture feels important and like a major lever of automated research. A prediction of pretraining research, at least in architecture and data selection to serve our current class of models, being automated in 2-3 years feels reasonable to me. All of this will be a massive trigger of Jevons paradox for agentic models. I expect demand to only increase, as the industry is largely bottlenecked on figuring out better ways to orient and deliver the agents. Meta’s Muse agent is an early indicator of this and we should expect more Muse-like experiences for different audiences and target use-cases. It’s value created by understanding how agents work, rather than pushing the frontier of performance. The equivalent phase in the broader scientific literature like biology and chemistry will be an era defined by models finding numerous cross-sub-field findings. The AI models are superhuman at crawling literature and making connections across sparse networks which are currently stewarded by small communities of scientists who rarely interacted. There will be a fine line between this heralding a new era of scientific discovery, e.g. with cures of most cancers, or an acceleration of the arc science was already on. Another industrial-scale piece of low-hanging fruit is improving the general quality of RL environments. You don’t have to look far to see another new RL data company that’s crossed $100M or $1B in revenue. There are way more than I expected. The average outputs from this sector are remarkably low-quality. Countless researchers agree that lots of what they buy is frankly crap. At the same time, the leading labs see clear return on investment from buying the data. The way that many RL environments are cruddy is clearly fixable. Read more

items.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
items.content: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner. Codex voice mode I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like: I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing: Start dev server and open in browser This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress. Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked. Talking to my computer I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources. Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex: Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want it on the tag pages. I don't want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they're... published, like once they're made public a month after they've gone out, I want them to show up on my search results. Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist . We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code. What we built We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice: A new model and migration to represent imported newsletters in Django, plus Django Admin configuration for that Four working imports: The most recent Substack items via RSS Every other Substack item via their undocumented API, which GPT-6 Astra knew about (it tried /api/v1/archive directly) and then ran a search to figure out how to paginate it and found this article by Karen Spinner All of my published monthly newsletters from my simonw/monthly-newsletter-archive GitHub repository My most recent private sponsors-only newsletter from a private repository The /newsletters/ and /newsletters/2026/ public archive pages Newsletters showing up on day and month archive pages too, but not on tag pages or my homepage Weekly Substack newsletters link to Substack; archived monthly newsletters have their own pages Integration with my site search engine It was almost ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I'd have to sit at the keyboard for a while. Finishing it with a review Once I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request. I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead. You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR . I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR. The end result You can see the end result at the new newsletters index page , or view the page for a previous monthly newsletter . The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages.
